title: The Case Suffixes
summary: Telugu marks the work a noun does by gluing a suffix onto it. The suffixes are few, regular, and separable — a different arrangement from the fused endings of a European declension, and an easier one.

rules.heading: Suffixes Are Glued, Not Fused
rules.statement: Telugu is an **agglutinative** language: it marks grammar by adding suffixes that keep their own shape and can be peeled off again. A Lithuanian ending fuses case and number into one syllable that cannot be divided; a Telugu suffix is a separate piece added to a stem that is still recognisable. It follows that the same case suffix is used with every noun, and that learning it once is learning it for all.
footnotes: The suffixes may also stack: a plural ending and then a case suffix after it, which a fused declension cannot do.

rules.heading: The Accusative — ని / ను
rules.statement: The direct object of a verb takes **-ని** or **-ను**. The suffix is used chiefly where the object is a **person or an animal**; where it is a lifeless thing, Telugu commonly leaves the noun bare, and the word order alone shows what is the object. This is a real difference from the European accusative, which is written whether the object breathes or not.

examples.note: a person, so the suffix is used
a thing, so the noun stands bare

rules.heading: The Dative — కి / కు
rules.statement: **-కి** or **-కు** marks the person to whom or for whom, and it is the busiest suffix in the language. Beside the indirect object it does work that English gives to a subject: with it Telugu says that a thing is liked, is needed, or is *had* — the last being the ordinary way of saying *have*, since Telugu has no such verb (¶65).

paradigms.caption: The dative of the pronouns
paradigms.footnote: **-కి** follows a front vowel and **-కు** a back one; the choice is one of sound, not of meaning.

rules.heading: The Locative — లో
rules.statement: **-లో** means *in* or *inside*, and **-మీద** means *on*. Both are added to the noun exactly as -కి is, and neither is a preposition: nothing in Telugu stands before its noun in the way English *in* and *on* do. Where English puts a little word in front, Telugu puts a suffix behind.

rules.heading: With — తో
rules.statement: **-తో** covers both what English divides between *with* the instrument and *with* the companion: *written with a pen* and *came with a friend* take the same suffix. Telugu draws no line where English draws one.

rules.heading: From — నుండి
rules.statement: **-నుండి** (or **-నుంచి**, which is commoner in speech) means *from*, of place and of time alike. With it a learner can at last answer the question every foreigner is asked: *where are you from?*

rules.heading: The Stem Before a Suffix
rules.statement: Before a suffix, many nouns take a special form called the **oblique stem** — a stem that never appears alone and exists only to be built on. **ఇల్లు** has the oblique **ఇంటి-**, so that *in the house* is **ఇంట్లో** and *to the house* **ఇంటికి**. This is the one real difficulty in the case system: the suffixes are regular, and it is the stems that must be learned.

paradigms.caption: Nominative and oblique
paradigms.footnote: A noun whose oblique differs from its nominative should be learned with both, as a Lithuanian noun is learned with its genitive.

drills.explanation: The oblique stem of నేను is నా-, and the dative suffix is added to that: *నాకు*. Adding -కు to the nominative gives a form that does not exist.
-నుండి, or -నుంచి in speech. -మీద means *on* and -ని marks a direct object.

drills.stem: What does it mean to say that Telugu is **agglutinative**?
options: That its words are very long.
That grammatical suffixes keep their own shape and can be separated from the stem.
That its endings fuse case and number into one syllable.
drills.explanation: The last option describes a fusional language such as Lithuanian, where one ending carries case and number together and cannot be divided. A Telugu suffix is a separate piece, the same on every noun.

drills.stem: Why is there no word standing **before** the noun in *పుస్తకంలో* (in the book)?
options: Because the word for *in* has been left out.
Because Telugu puts after the noun what English puts before it.
Because పుస్తకం is a special noun.
Because the phrase is in the plural.
drills.explanation: -లో is a suffix, not a preposition. Telugu has postpositions and suffixes and no prepositions at all — the head follows what depends on it throughout the language.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly formed?
drills.explanation: Each pronoun has an oblique stem — నా-, నీ-, మీ- — and the dative is built on that. *నేనుకు* adds the suffix to the nominative, which Telugu never does.

drills.stem: *నేను పుస్తకం చదువుతున్నాను* has no suffix on **పుస్తకం**, though it is the object. Why not?
options: Because the sentence is in the present.
Because the object is a lifeless thing, and Telugu commonly leaves such an object bare.
Because పుస్తకం cannot take a suffix.
Because the suffix has been dropped in error.
drills.explanation: The accusative -ని is used chiefly of people and animals. A lifeless object usually stands bare, the word order showing what it is — a distinction the European accusative does not make.

drills.stem: How would you say **with a friend**?
drills.explanation: -తో covers both the instrument and the companion — *with a pen* and *with a friend* alike. The others give *to*, *in* and *from*.

drills.stem: *ఇల్లు* becomes *ఇంటికి* in the dative. What has happened?
options: The suffix is irregular for this noun.
The noun has taken its oblique stem ఇంటి- before the regular suffix.
drills.explanation: The suffix -కి is perfectly regular; it is the **stem** that changes. This is the real labour of the Telugu case system, and why a noun with an unpredictable oblique should be learned with it, as a Lithuanian noun is learned with its genitive.

drills.stem: Which statements contrast Telugu with a fusional language such as Lithuanian?
options: A Telugu case suffix keeps one shape across all nouns.
A Telugu suffix can be separated from the stem it is added to.
Telugu fuses case and number into a single ending.
Telugu places its case markers after the noun rather than before.
drills.explanation: Fusing case and number into one indivisible ending is exactly what Lithuanian does and Telugu does not: Telugu adds the plural, then the case, each keeping its own shape.

drills.stem: **నేను ఇంట్లో ఉన్నాను** — how many of its three words carry a case suffix?
drills.explanation: One: *ఇంట్లో*, the oblique ఇంటి- with -లో. *నేను* is the bare nominative subject, which takes no suffix at all, and the third word is the verb. Counting two usually means mistaking the nominative for a marked case.

drills.stem: How many **different case suffixes** does this section teach?
drills.explanation: Five: -ని for the object, -కి for the dative, -లో for the locative, -తో for *with*, -నుండి for *from*. Each is the same on every noun; it is the stems in front of them that vary.

drills.title: నా ఊరు
drills.passage: నా పేరు రవి. నేను ఒక చిన్న ఊరు నుండి. ఇప్పుడు నేను హైదరాబాద్‌లో ఉన్నాను. నాకు ఇక్కడ ఒక ఇల్లు ఉంది. ఇంట్లో నా పుస్తకాలు ఉన్నాయి. నేను స్నేహితుడితో ఇక్కడ ఉన్నాను. మా ఇంటికి రండి!
drills.translation: My name is Ravi. I am from a small town. Now I am in Hyderabad. I have a house here. My books are in the house. I am here with a friend. Come to our house!

questions.explanation: *నేను ఒక చిన్న ఊరు నుండి* — the suffix -నుండి marks where he comes from. Hyderabad is where he is now, which the locative -లో marks instead.
*ఇప్పుడు నేను హైదరాబాద్‌లో ఉన్నాను* — the same locative -లో as ఇంట్లో, glued this time to the city's name rather than to *ఇల్లు*.

questions.stem: Which words in the passage carry the suffix meaning **in**?
questions.explanation: -లో is *in*. *ఇంటికి* is the dative, *to the house*, and *స్నేహితుడితో* takes -తో, *with*. All four are built on the same principle and differ only in the suffix glued on.

questions.stem: The passage uses the word for *house* three times — **ఇల్లు**, **ఇంట్లో**, **ఇంటికి**. How many distinct case suffixes are used with it?
questions.explanation: Two: -లో and -కి. The first occurrence, *ఇల్లు*, is the bare nominative and carries none. Both suffixed forms are built on the oblique ఇంటి-, which never appears alone (¶63).
